History timeline

Church History Timeline

Historical context identifies the history being described. Who affirms this? compares the specific teaching named on each card, with sources in its details.

Agreement with a teaching does not necessarily mean acceptance of the council’s authority or every canon. “Not established here” means the cited sources do not settle that group’s position.

Search and filter
Chronological order; spacing is not proportional to years.

42 of 108 events

Early Church

30–799

Early Christian history precedes the later divisions. Reception labels below identify agreement or disagreement about each selected teaching.

First century (c. 30–33)
Context: Early ChurchHistorical event

Acts describes the gift of the Holy Spirit, St. Peter’s preaching, Baptism, and the common life of the first believers. The calendar year is approximate.

Text: Acts 2

Historical event or source witness. Placement in this timeline does not imply that every church endorses every statement or practice associated with it.

c. 49
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

The apostles and elders consider Gentile converts and circumcision. Their letter does not impose the full Mosaic ceremonial law on Gentiles. The date is approximate.

Text: Acts 15:28–29

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Gentile converts are not required to undergo Mosaic circumcision

This comparison concerns admission without circumcision. It does not settle every later interpretation of the council’s dietary directions.

  • Eastern OrthodoxGentiles admitted without circumcision
  • Roman CatholicGentiles admitted without circumcision
  • Westminster ReformedMosaic ceremonial obligations abrogated
  • Anglican ArticlesMosaic ceremonial obligations do not bind Christians
325
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

The council rejects Arius’s teaching that the Son is a creature and confesses the Son as of one substance with the Father. It also issues disciplinary canons.

Text: Nicene Creed (325)

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: The Son’s full divinity and being of one essence with the Father

The comparison concerns the creed’s teaching about the Son. Agreement here does not mean acceptance of every disciplinary canon.

  • Eastern OrthodoxReceived as an ecumenical council
  • Roman CatholicDoctrine and ecumenical council affirmed
  • Westminster ReformedDoctrine affirmed; council authority qualified
  • Anglican ArticlesCreedal doctrine affirmed; councils may err
  • Coptic Orthodox (Oriental Orthodox family)Council received
381
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

The council reaffirms Nicaea and condemns teachings denying the Holy Spirit’s divinity. The creed received under this council’s name confesses the Spirit as Lord and giver of life, worshipped with the Father and Son.

Text: Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed; Canon 1

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: The Holy Spirit’s full divinity and the Nicene–Constantinopolitan Creed

Agreement on the Spirit’s divinity must be distinguished from the later Filioque addition and disputes over its theology.

  • Eastern OrthodoxReceived as an ecumenical council
  • Roman CatholicSpirit’s divinity and council affirmed
  • Westminster ReformedDoctrine affirmed; council authority qualified
  • Anglican ArticlesCreedal doctrine affirmed; councils may err
  • Coptic Orthodox (Oriental Orthodox family)Council received
431
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

The council condemns Nestorius and approves St. Cyril’s teaching on the unity of the incarnate Word. Calling Mary Theotokos safeguards the confession that the one born from her is God the Word made flesh.

Text: Approval of St. Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: The one divine person of the incarnate Word; Mary as Theotokos

Theotokos identifies the person born of Mary as God the Word. This comparison does not assign later Marian doctrines to all groups.

  • Eastern OrthodoxReceived as an ecumenical council
  • Roman CatholicDoctrine and ecumenical council affirmed
  • Westminster ReformedOne-person Christology affirmed; Theotokos title not assessed
  • Anglican ArticlesOne-person Christology affirmed; Theotokos title not assessed
  • Coptic Orthodox (Oriental Orthodox family)Council received
451
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

The definition confesses one and the same Christ in two natures, fully divine and fully human. Its reception is disputed, contributing to the enduring separation between the Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian churches.

Text: Definition of Chalcedon

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: One and the same Christ in two natures, divine and human

The comparison distinguishes agreement about Christ’s divinity and humanity from formal reception of Chalcedon and its terminology.

  • Eastern OrthodoxReceived as an ecumenical council
  • Roman CatholicDoctrine and ecumenical council affirmed
  • Westminster ReformedDoctrine affirmed; council authority qualified
  • Anglican ArticlesCreedal doctrine affirmed; councils may err
  • Coptic Orthodox (Oriental Orthodox family)Council not received
680–681
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

Against Monothelitism, the council confesses two natural wills and two natural operations in the one Christ. His human will is preserved and freely follows his divine will.

Text: Definition of Faith (680–681)

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Christ’s divine and human natural wills and operations

The precise ruling concerns two natural wills and operations in the one Christ, not two persons or opposing moral purposes.

  • Eastern OrthodoxReceived as an ecumenical council
  • Roman CatholicDoctrine and ecumenical council affirmed
  • Westminster ReformedExact two-will reception not established here
787
Context: Early ChurchTeaching / ruling

The council restores the veneration of holy icons and distinguishes this honor from the worship belonging to God alone. Honor given to an image passes to the person represented.

Text: Definition of Faith on holy images

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Legitimate holy images and their veneration, distinguished from the worship due to God

The comparison concerns religious images and veneration. Permitting art and venerating an icon are different questions.

  • Eastern OrthodoxReceived as an ecumenical council
  • Roman CatholicIcon veneration affirmed
  • Westminster ReformedReligious images and image-mediated worship rejected
  • Anglican ArticlesHistorical image-devotion condemned

Medieval

800–1499
843
Context: Early ChurchHistorical event

Under Empress Theodora and Patriarch Methodius, icons are restored after the second iconoclast period. Eastern Orthodoxy commemorates this restoration on the first Sunday of Great Lent.

Text: Restoration of the decisions of Nicaea II

Historical event or source witness. Placement in this timeline does not imply that every church endorses every statement or practice associated with it.

1014
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

John Paul II’s historical account dates the addition of the Filioque to Rome’s Creed to Henry II’s coronation in 1014. Earlier Latin use preceded Rome’s adoption. The Catholic catechism acknowledges continuing Orthodox disagreement over its introduction into the Creed.

Text: Roman liturgical adoption of the Filioque

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: The Filioque in the Creed

The comparison concerns the Spirit’s eternal procession and the added words, not whether the 1014 liturgical adoption occurred.

  • Roman CatholicLatin doctrine affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxAddition rejected
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Procession from Father and Son affirmed
1054
Context: Eastern Orthodox historyHistorical event

Roman legates and the Constantinopolitan synod exchange personal excommunications amid accumulated disputes. The date marks a stage in a prolonged estrangement; it is not a single act that instantly separated every Eastern and Western Christian.

Text: Censures of July 1054

Historical event or source witness. Placement in this timeline does not imply that every church endorses every statement or practice associated with it.

Trenham note
1075
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

Twenty-seven propositions in Gregory VII’s register articulate extensive papal authority. The manuscript position is dated 1075; authorship and intended use require care. The text is evidence of Gregorian claims, rather than a universally received ecumenical ruling.

Text: Dictatus Papae, propositions 1–3, 12, 19

Trenham note

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Universal papal authority claims

The comparison selects the claim to universal papal authority; it is not a verdict on all 27 propositions, including medieval political claims.

  • Roman CatholicUniversal primacy affirmed; document scope limited
  • Eastern OrthodoxPapal supremacy rejected
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Papal headship rejected
1204
Context: Eastern Orthodox historyHistorical event

Crusaders sack Constantinople, plunder churches, and establish Latin rule and a Latin patriarch. The destruction deepens the estrangement between Greek Christians and the Latin West.

Historical event or source witness. Placement in this timeline does not imply that every church endorses every statement or practice associated with it.

Trenham note
1215
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

The Western council’s confession described Eucharistic change of substance. Its disciplinary constitutions required annual confession and Easter communion, regulated clergy and education, and asserted Roman ecclesiastical order. These are Latin conciliar decisions, not a council received as ecumenical by the Orthodox Church.

Text: Constitutions 1 and 21

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Eucharistic change and Lateran IV’s authority

Rows compare the confession of Eucharistic change in constitution 1. Annual confession and the council’s other disciplinary canons require separate assessment.

  • Roman CatholicCouncil’s Eucharistic definition affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxReal presence affirmed; council not received as ecumenical
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Transubstantiation rejected
  • Lutheran (Augsburg Confession)True Body and Blood affirmed; different evidential scope
1274
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

At Lyons the Latin council restated the procession of the Spirit from Father and Son as one principle. A union with Byzantine representatives was proclaimed. Its decree records the Latin doctrinal position; proclamation of union did not secure enduring East–West communion.

Text: Constitution on the procession of the Holy Spirit

Trenham note

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Lyons II’s Filioque formula

The doctrinal comparison concerns procession from Father and Son as one principle. Proclaiming political or ecclesial union is a separate historical fact.

  • Roman CatholicLatin formula affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxFilioque addition rejected
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Shared procession formula; council authority qualified
1302
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

In conflict with royal power, Boniface VIII asserted one Church, the subordination of temporal power to spiritual power, and the necessity of subjection to the Roman pontiff. The bull is a primary statement of medieval papal claims, not an Orthodox ecclesiological definition.

Text: Unam Sanctam, 18 November 1302

Trenham note

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Roman subjection and salvation

The comparison concerns the bull’s concluding claim about subjection to the Roman pontiff. Its medieval two-swords political argument is not treated as a single modern dogma.

  • Roman CatholicRoman primacy affirmed; salvation claim requires context
  • Eastern OrthodoxUniversal Roman supremacy rejected
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Roman headship rejected
1341–1351
Context: Eastern Orthodox historyTeaching / ruling

Councils in Constantinople defend St. Gregory Palamas’s account of participation in God’s uncreated energies while God’s essence remains inaccessible. These are later Orthodox synods, not additional councils within the traditional list of seven ecumenical councils.

Text: Constantinopolitan synods of 1341, 1347, and 1351

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: The distinction between God’s unknowable essence and uncreated energies

This is later Orthodox synodal teaching; acceptance of general language about grace or union with God does not prove agreement with every Palamite formulation.

  • Eastern OrthodoxTeaching affirmed by later Orthodox councils
  • Other churchesReception not established in this entry
1439
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

Laetentur caeli addressed the Filioque, Eucharistic bread, purification after death, and Roman primacy. Most Greek delegates signed; St. Mark of Ephesus declined. The decree did not secure lasting general Orthodox reception.

Text: Laetentur caeli, 6 July 1439

Trenham note

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Florence’s definition of Roman primacy

These rows compare Roman primacy in the decree with the Greeks. Filioque, Eucharistic bread, and purification after death are additional teachings, not covered by one blanket verdict.

  • Roman CatholicUniversal Roman primacy affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxUnion not received; supremacy rejected
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Universal Roman headship rejected
29 May 1453
Context: Eastern Orthodox historyHistorical event

Ottoman forces capture Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire. Orthodox church life continues under changed political conditions. This is a political watershed, rather than a new doctrinal ruling.

Historical event or source witness. Placement in this timeline does not imply that every church endorses every statement or practice associated with it.

Reformations

1500–1599
1517
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

Luther circulated theses disputing indulgence preaching and papal authority over penalties. This marks a conventional starting point for the Reformation, rather than the founding of a fully developed Lutheran denomination.

Text: Ninety-Five Theses

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Indulgences and their claimed power

Luther’s 1517 propositions about indulgences, not his later complete theology or a universal Protestant confession.

  • Martin Luther in 1517Indulgence claims challenged
  • Roman CatholicIndulgences retained; forgiveness distinguished
  • Eastern OrthodoxFormal reception not established
1523
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

The first Zurich disputation placed Zwingli’s Sixty-Seven Articles before the city council. Swiss reform developed alongside the Lutheran movement, with differences that would become especially visible over the Eucharist.

Text: Sixty-Seven Articles

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: The Eucharist as remembrance rather than a sacrifice

Article XVIII’s denial of the Mass as sacrifice; not a claim that Orthodox or Catholic worship repeats the Crucifixion.

  • Zwingli’s Zurich ArticlesMemorial account asserted
  • Eastern OrthodoxDenial of Eucharistic sacrifice rejected
  • Roman CatholicDenial of Eucharistic sacrifice rejected
1525
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and George Blaurock participated in believers’ baptisms in Zurich. This is a major beginning of Swiss Anabaptism; the wider Anabaptist movement had several regional beginnings.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1529
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

Luther and Zwingli met at Marburg. Their substantial agreement did not resolve whether Christ’s body and blood are bodily present in the Supper; the disagreement obstructed a united evangelical alliance.

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Disagreement about Christ’s bodily presence in the Supper

The historical dispute and later representative confessional contrast; one Lutheran eyewitness is not treated as an impartial statement of every Swiss position.

  • Luther’s party at MarburgBodily presence maintained
  • Zwingli and Oecolampadius at MarburgLutheran account not accepted
  • Later Protestant confessionsLutheran and Reformed accounts differ
1530
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

Melanchthon presented the Lutheran confession at the imperial Diet. Its teaching on justification and the Lord’s Supper is a confessional reference point for Lutheran churches and differs from later Reformed formulations.

Text: Augsburg Confession

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Faith alone as the means of justification

This comparison concerns the named teaching, not acceptance of the whole document, every canon, or the issuing body’s authority.

  • Augsburg Lutheran confessionJustification through faith affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxFaith alone rejected
  • Roman CatholicExclusion of cooperation rejected
1534
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

Parliament recognized Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church of England, rejecting papal jurisdiction. Later reigns brought major doctrinal and liturgical changes; the 1534 jurisdictional break alone did not settle Anglican theology.

Text: Act of Supremacy

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1536
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

The first edition of Calvin’s Institutes appeared at Basel. He repeatedly enlarged the work, reaching its major final Latin edition in 1559; later Reformed churches were not simply founded by this single publication.

Text: Institutes of the Christian Religion

Publication of the 1536 first edition, subsequently enlarged. No agreement labels are assigned to the entire work, and formulations from later editions are not imported into this event.

1545–1563
Context: Western / Roman Catholic historyTeaching / ruling

In three periods between 1545 and 1563, Trent defined Catholic teaching amid Reformation controversy and enacted reforms. Its decrees addressed Scripture and traditions, justification, and the sacraments. These Latin definitions answer Protestant claims while remaining distinct from Orthodox conciliar teaching.

Text: Sessions IV (1546), VI (1547), XIII (1551), and later decrees

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Trent’s authority and selected Reformation disputes

Trent issued many definitions. These rows identify reception of the council and the selected Scripture/tradition, justification, and Eucharistic texts shown below.

  • Roman CatholicCatholic definitions affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxNot received as ecumenical; individual teachings require comparison
  • Reformed / Presbyterian (Westminster)Selected definitions contested
1560
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

The Scottish Parliament adopted the confession drafted by Knox and five colleagues. Reformed doctrine and subsequent Presbyterian organization developed in Scotland; Westminster later replaced this confession as the principal Scottish doctrinal standard.

Text: Scots Confession

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Christ as true God and true man in one person

Only the Christology of Article VI is compared. Agreement with this doctrine does not mean acceptance of the Scots Confession as a confessional authority.

  • Scots Reformed confessionTwo-nature Christology affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxChalcedonian doctrine affirmed
  • Roman CatholicChalcedonian doctrine affirmed
1563
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

Commissioned in the Electoral Palatinate, Heidelberg teaches Christian faith through questions and answers arranged around guilt, grace, and gratitude. Its discussions of faith, good works, baptism, and the Supper remain central to many Reformed churches.

Text: Heidelberg Catechism

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Bread and wine do not become Christ’s actual body and blood

The contrast concerns conversion of the elements, not whether Reformed believers claim any true spiritual communion with Christ.

  • Heidelberg Reformed catechismConversion of the elements denied
  • Eastern OrthodoxReal change of the gifts affirmed
  • Roman CatholicTransubstantiation affirmed
1566
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

Bullinger’s confession was published and received by Swiss and other Reformed churches. It treats Scripture, councils, salvation, the church, sacraments, worship, and civil government in an extensive doctrinal statement.

Text: Second Helvetic Confession

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Propitiatory sacrifice in the Eucharist

The selected teaching is the confession’s rejection of the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice; this does not assess every doctrine in the confession.

  • Second Helvetic Reformed confessionPropitiatory Mass rejected
  • Eastern OrthodoxDenial of Eucharistic sacrifice rejected
  • Roman CatholicDenial of Eucharistic sacrifice rejected
1571
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

The Articles developed from earlier Tudor formularies; the 1571 settlement made subscription a requirement for clergy. They provide an Anglican doctrinal standard alongside the Prayer Book and episcopal order.

Text: Thirty-Nine Articles

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Transubstantiation and reception of Christ in the Supper

The historic Articles’ Eucharistic formulations are compared; this is not a claim that all present-day Anglicans explain the Supper identically.

  • Church of England’s ArticlesTransubstantiation rejected
  • Eastern OrthodoxReal change of the gifts affirmed
  • Roman CatholicTransubstantiation affirmed
c. 1575–1581
Context: Eastern Orthodox historyHistorical event

Lutheran theologians send the Augsburg Confession in Greek to Patriarch Jeremias II. Their correspondence tests proposed agreement and records substantial disagreements. The OCA account dates the main exchange to about 1575–1581.

Text: Responses of Patriarch Jeremias II to the Augsburg Confession

Historical event or source witness. Placement in this timeline does not imply that every church endorses every statement or practice associated with it.

Confessions and churches

1600–1749
1609
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

An English Separatist congregation in Amsterdam adopted believers’ baptism under John Smyth. Helwys and others subsequently developed the English General Baptist stream, distinguished from later Particular Baptists by their understanding of Christ’s atonement.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1618–1619
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

An international Reformed synod rejected the Remonstrants’ positions and adopted the Canons of Dort. The canons address disputed points, not the whole of Reformed doctrine; their five headings are not a complete Protestant catechism.

Text: Canons of Dort

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Election is not conditioned on foreseen faith

The selected issue is the basis of election, not a complete comparison of every Reformed or Catholic account of grace.

  • Dort Reformed confessionUnconditional election affirmed
  • Remonstrants of 1610Faith and perseverance specified
  • Eastern OrthodoxAbsolute predestination rejected
  • Roman CatholicWhole-system judgment not established
1646–1647
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

The Westminster Assembly completed its confession in 1646; the Church of Scotland adopted it in 1647. Its reception shaped Presbyterian standards, while Congregationalists and Particular Baptists later adapted its structure with important changes.

Text: Westminster Confession of Faith

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Two sacraments of the Gospel

This compares the number and classification of sacraments; it does not claim all uses of the word sacrament are equivalent.

  • Westminster Reformed; PCA editionTwo sacraments affirmed
  • Eastern OrthodoxSeven Mysteries enumerated
  • Roman CatholicSeven sacraments enumerated
March 1672
Context: Eastern Orthodox historyTeaching / ruling

The synod under Patriarch Dositheus rejects the Calvinist confession attributed to Lucaris and adopts its own eighteen decrees. It addresses Scripture, predestination, justification, Church authority, and the sacraments. This is a later Orthodox synod, outside the seven-council list.

Text: Confession of Dositheus; eighteen decrees and four questions

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Justification, predestination and Eucharistic change in Dositheus’s confession

The comparison names particular doctrines in the eighteen decrees; it does not treat this later Orthodox synod as one of the seven ecumenical councils.

  • Orthodox synod of Jerusalem/BethlehemAnti-Calvinist confession adopted
  • Westminster ReformedContrary formulations in the named doctrines
  • Anglican ArticlesFaith-only justification; transubstantiation rejected
1738
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

John Wesley’s experience at a London religious society became a defining memory of Methodist renewal. Wesley remained an Anglican priest; this event did not itself establish a separate Methodist denomination.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

Modern movements

1750–present
1784
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

The Christmas Conference organized the Methodist Episcopal Church in Baltimore. The new American church gave institutional form to a movement that had originated within Anglicanism, in circumstances changed by the American Revolution.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1831–1832
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

The Stone and Campbell movements joined in Kentucky. The union is commonly dated 1832; the Disciples’ chronology records the representative handshake on December 31, 1831. Later Christian Churches, Churches of Christ, and Disciples developed within this broader family.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1906–1909
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles became a major center of the emerging Pentecostal movement. Earlier events at Topeka in 1901 also figure in its history; Pentecostalism subsequently developed several doctrinal and organizational streams.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1914
Context: Protestant historyHistorical event

Pentecostal ministers and believers met in Hot Springs, Arkansas, and organized the Assemblies of God. The fellowship grew within the wider Pentecostal movement; its organization was not the beginning of all Pentecostal Christianity.

Historical event, institutional development, or publication. This card does not assign doctrinal agreement or disagreement.

1999
Context: Protestant historyTeaching / ruling

The Lutheran World Federation and the Roman Catholic Church signed the Joint Declaration in Augsburg. It reports a consensus on basic truths of justification while addressing remaining differences; its signatories do not represent every Protestant church.

Text: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification

Who affirms this?

Teaching compared: Consensus in basic truths of justification

The declaration applies to its stated dialogue partners and the teachings as presented in it, not every Protestant body or every historic formulation.

  • Subscribing Lutheran churches and Roman Catholic ChurchQualified consensus affirmed
  • Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran SynodClaim of agreement contested
  • Eastern OrthodoxNot a subscribing body in this document
